reading.body:
AI risk is being underwritten without claims history, so insurers are pricing it from live telemetry, continuous audits and simulated losses instead.

The pattern across these ten mechanisms is a shift in what gets measured. Automated property underwriting uses vision models and sensor analytics to price data centre risk directly, and telemetry-based dynamic premiums adjust against thermals, humidity and load variation. Parametric downtime payouts settle automatically when temperature or power crosses a defined threshold, with no loss adjustment. The rated object is increasingly the physical facility and its power and cooling behaviour, not the software running inside it.

For AI specifically, the exposure is correlated in a way ordinary property risk is not. Reinsurers are modelling catastrophic loss where one foundational model failure reaches millions of businesses at once, which turns a single point of failure into an accumulation problem. Usage-based policy limits scale with active GPU consumption and deployment footprint, so the size of the cover tracks compute directly. Governance maturity discounts and red teaming as a policy condition make safety auditing a price input rather than a compliance formality, and third party safety rating agencies would extend the credit rating pattern to model safety, deciding underwriting eligibility.

What the data does not supply is scale. There are no premium figures, no named insurers or reinsurers, no jurisdictions, and no indication of which of these mechanisms are in force rather than proposed. The no historical data problem is named as the central difficulty but not resolved here. Synthetic loss scenario forecasting is offered as the answer to pricing rare failure modes that have never occurred, and whether simulation is an adequate substitute for experience is exactly the question the list raises and leaves open.
